title: Architecture Standards: API, Code, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance & ADRs
author: Priya Rao
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also describes the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process and summarizes recent decisions relevant to these areas. The goal is to provide a single, opinionated reference for teams building production-grade inference services and control-plane components.

Goals

- Ensure consistency across services so integrations, onboarding, and ops are predictable.
- Reduce operational and cognitive overhead through shared conventions (APIs, metrics, rollout patterns).
- Make performance and cost trade-offs explicit and reviewable via ADRs.
- Provide actionable templates and checklists for safe rollouts and incident response.

Scope

Applies to all Redwood services and customer-facing endpoints in hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, including: control plane APIs, serving runtime components, inference routers, autoscalers, and developer-facing SDK/endpoints. Does not directly replace language-specific style guides (those are referenced below).

1) API Standards

Summary

APIs should be stable, discoverable, and backwards-compatible where possible. Prioritize clear error semantics and observable request metadata so downstream tooling (billing, tracing, policy) can operate reliably.

Key rules

- Versioning: Use path-based versioning for public APIs: /v1/, /v2/. Internal service APIs may use header-based versioning for zero-downtime upgrades but must be documented.
- Resource names: kebab-case for REST paths (e.g., /v1/models/{model-id}/deployments).
- Idempotency: All mutating operations must accept an Idempotency-Key header and be idempotent for at least 24 hours.
- Error model: Follow RFC 7807 problem-details JSON schema. Required fields: type, title, status, detail, instance. Add machine-readable error_code (snake_case).
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for large result sets with next_cursor and prev_cursor fields. Avoid offset pagination for index endpoints.
- Rate limiting: 429 with Retry-After header; include X-RateLimit-* headers for quota visibility.
- Schemas: Publish OpenAPI (3.0+) for all public APIs and internal service contracts. Keep examples for common SDK calls.

Example: standard response error JSON

```json
{
  "type": "https://redwood.example.com/probs/validation",
  "title": "Invalid input",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Prompt exceeds max length for selected model",
  "instance": "/v1/generate/req_1234",
  "error_code": "prompt_max_length_exceeded"
}
```

Backward compatibility and deprecation

- Deprecation window: minimum 90 days for public APIs. Communicate via console, email, and changelog.
- Use feature flags and compatibility shims for server-side behavior changes when possible.

2) Coding Standards

Summary

Standard engineering practices to improve code quality, security, and maintainability across Redwood repos.

General rules

- Languages: Service implementations should use the language best fit for the problem (Go/Python/TypeScript/Rust). Each repo must have a top-level README specifying language, runtime, and supported versions.
- Linters & formatters: Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff for Python, and eslint/prettier for TypeScript. CI must fail the build for lint/format violations.
- Tests: Minimum coverage per service: 70% for critical infra code, 50% for user-facing features. All new features require unit and integration tests.
- PR process: Require two reviews for production-impacting changes; one reviewer must be from service owning team and one from platform (if applicable). Use CODEOWNERS to auto-request reviewers.
- Secrets: No secrets in source control. Use the secrets manager (vault or cloud KMS-backed) and the standard secrets injection library.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, Networking, Security)

Summary

Infra must be declarative, reproducible, and reviewed. Terraform is the canonical tool for cloud resources; Helm charts (or Kustomize) for Kubernetes manifests.

Standards and rules

- IaC repositories: Separate repos for platform-level infra and service-level infra. Use terraform workspaces for environment separation (prod/staging/dev).
- Modules: Common terraform modules maintained in infra-modules repo. Changes to modules require cross-team review and a rollout plan.
- Networking: Default deny networking posture. Use private subnets for internal services and NAT/gateway for outbound control. Customer data paths for Private deployments must be isolated within customer VPCs.
- Secrets & keys: KMS for encryption at rest. Rotate service keys every 90 days. Access via short-lived credentials (STS) where supported.
- Observability provisioning: Every environment must provision the standard set of metrics, traces, and log sinks per the observability section below.

Example Terraform snippet (VPC peering acceptor):

```hcl
resource "aws_vpc_peering_connection" "peer" {
  vpc_id        = var.vpc_id
  peer_vpc_id   = var.peer_vpc_id
n  auto_accept   = false
  tags = {
    Name = "redwood-peer-${var.env}"
  }
}
```

4) Model-Serving Standards

Summary

Standards for model packaging, versioning, rollout, and runtime configuration to ensure predictable latency, correctness, and cost.

Model packaging and registry

- Every model must have a manifest file (YAML) with fields: model_id, version, commit_sha, quantization_profile (if any), resource_requirements, artifact_location, owner_team, and compatibility matrix. Example manifest required for onboarding.
- Models are stored in the model-registry with immutable versioned artifacts. Deployments reference a model by manifest_id.

Runtime configuration

- Quantization profiles: Quantization profiles must be validated in a dedicated perf/regression job before promotion to production. Keep a canonical list of approved profiles per GPU type.
- KV cache and prefix caching: Default enabled for chat-style workloads. Cache TTL must be documented per route.

Rollout patterns and safety

- Canary deploy: 5% traffic for 24 hours, monitor latency and token-cost metrics and quality evals (prompt set pass rate). If no regressions, expand 25% for 12 hours, then to 100% at controlled pace.
- Automatic fallback: If P99 latency exceeds configured threshold or model error_rate > 0.5% for 10 min, automatically failover to a compatible variant (smaller model or CPU fallback) and create incident.

Deployment checklist (required)

1. Model manifest in registry.
2. Canary perf job and quality evaluation run.
3. Observability dashboard and alerts provisioned.
4. Rollout policy specified (timeouts, rollback criteria, fallback).
5. Owner and on-call listed.

5) Observability Standards

Summary

Observability enables fast debugging, SLO compliance, and billing/usage attribution. Standards focus on metric naming, tracing conventions, log structure, and retention.

Metrics

- Metric naming: dot-separated, lower_snake_case prefixed with service name: redwood.ingest.request_count, redwood.model.v1.latency_ms.p95.
- Required metrics per service: request_count, request_errors, request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, cpu_usage_pct, gpu_utilization_pct, batch_size_distribution.
- Tags/labels: include environment, region, service, model_id, route, customer_id (for dedicated/private where applicable).

Tracing

- Use W3C Trace-Context headers. Root span must include request_type, model_id, route, and user_tier. Spans for heavy operations (model forward, KV cache lookup, disk IO) must be instrumented.

Logging

- Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, trace_id, span_id, request_id, msg, extra (map of contextual keys). Redact PII and secrets at emit time.

Dashboards & alerts

- Standard dashboard template: traffic, latency distribution, error breakdown, cost-by-token, and autoscaler health.
- Alerts: SLO burn rate alerts, high error rate alert (>1% sustained 5m), P99 latency breach, and sudden drop in request_count. Alert severity and runbooks must be linked to each alert.

Retention

- Traces: 30 days. Metrics: 90 days full resolution, 365 days aggregated. Logs: 90 days default; extended retention is an add-on.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

SLOs (applies to hosted API and Dedicated control-plane endpoints)

- Latency SLOs (per-route, per-model-class): P95 < 200ms for small models (<4B) on hosted tier; P95 < 400ms for medium models (4B-13B); P95 < 900ms for large models (>13B) where GPU resource limits apply. P99 targets are 2x P95.
- Availability SLO: 99.9% for hosted public API endpoints (monthly). Dedicated customer-facing endpoints may negotiate higher SLAs.
- Throughput targets: Each node template must document expected tokens/sec and effective concurrency for typical prompt lengths.

Autoscaling and cost controls

- Autoscaling cooldowns: scale up cooldown 30s, scale down cooldown 2m for GPU pools. Batching parameters should be tuned with a simulation job to avoid latency regressions.
- Cost-aware routing: traffic may be routed to cheaper model variants during non-peak hours per routing policy. Such policies must be documented and explicitly opt-in for customer workloads.

Performance testing

- Benchmarking suite: Every major change that touches the runtime or critical kernels requires running the benchmarking-and-perf-suite (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Keep public benchmark artifacts in the perf-artifacts bucket.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process

Process summary

- Use ADRs for architectural decisions that have long-lived impact (model format, kernel selection, major runtime changes, infra assumptions).
- ADR template required: title, status (proposed/accepted/deprecated), context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered, owner, date. Store ADRs under confluence and in the code repo in docs/adrs/.
- Review: ADRs affecting multiple teams must be reviewed by impacted owners and recorded reviewers (minimum 2 reviewers).

Recent ADRs (summary table)

- ADR-2025-08: "Standardize model manifest schema v1" — Decision: Adopt YAML manifest v1 with immutable versioning and artifact checksum. Owner: Priya Rao. Status: accepted. Link: /adrs/ADR-2025-08
- ADR-2025-11: "Fallback policy default" — Decision: Default automatic fallback to compatible model variant with throttled traffic redirection. Owner: Anders Svensson. Status: accepted. Link: /adrs/ADR-2025-11
- ADR-2026-01: "Observability retention and aggregation tiers" — Decision: Traces 30d, metrics 90d/365d aggregated. Owner: Marissa Kim. Status: accepted. Link: /adrs/ADR-2026-01

How to contribute an ADR

1. Draft ADR in docs/adrs/ using the template.
2. Create a PR targeting the service repo. Include impact analysis and migration plan.
3. Request reviewers: owner_team leads and platform reviewers. Allow 7 business days for review.
4. After acceptance, publish in Confluence with cross-links and schedule a follow-up migration/rollout if applicable.

Appendix: Templates and checklists

- Model manifest template (YAML):

```yaml
model_id: "gptx-13b"
version: "2026-01-18"
commit_sha: "abc123def"
quantization_profile: "int8-q4"
resource_requirements:
  gpu: "a100-40gb"
  memory_gb: 60
artifact_location: "s3://model-registry/gptx-13b/2026-01-18"
owner_team: "eng-serving-runtime"
compatibility:
  - runtime: "v2.1"
    supported_sequence_lengths: [512, 1024, 2048]
```

- Rollout checklist (short): manifest, perf regression run, canary policy, dashboard + alerts, rollback plan, owner oncall.
